lines: The oven, two big decks of it, ticking as it warms. Whatever is in it, the whole kitchen smells of it.
Laura keeps a timer on a string round her neck, and has never once needed it.
Steel work tables all along the wall: the big stand mixer, a scale that weighs to the gram, and a bench scraper worn smooth from years of good use.
The recipes are on index cards in a tin, and the cards are older than some of the customers.
Two fridges and a chest freezer, humming in three different keys: butter by the case, eggs by the flat, cream, and a tub of lemon curd for tomorrow.
Everything in here is going to be a cookie or a cake by the end of the week.

The cake table, where the custom cakes get built: a turntable, offset spatulas, a rack of food colours. There's a sketch taped up of somebody's birthday cake, three tiers, and it's going to be exactly that.
Weddings, birthdays, a retirement, a dog's first birthday once. If you can describe it, it gets made.
A rolling rack of trays, cooling: lemon shortbread cookies, every tray of them. People can't get enough — they go out front by the dozen and they're gone.
Buttery, a little sharp, sugar on top. One is never the number.

people.name: Laura
lines: Lemon shortbread — that's the batch cooling. Third one today, and it still won't be enough; they go about as fast as they get out front.

That's a birthday cake on the table for tomorrow, three tiers, and it'll look just like the drawing. The cakes are my own business — orders come to me, and the shop lets me build them in here once they've locked up. Weddings too, and whatever else somebody dreams up.
Some nights I'm in here late, after the shop's closed, when the place is quiet and the oven's all mine. It suits us both — they get a baker, I get a kitchen, and nobody's in anybody's way.
